# Three- and four-level lasers {#sec-pumping} [![Open in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/{{< var github_user >}}/{{< var repo >}}/blob/main/{{< var subdir >}}/notebooks/pumping.ipynb){.colab-link}  Run this chapter's code in Google Colab (no installation). *Slides 11–14 (the laser principle with the ruby laser, three-level lasers, the four-level Nd:YAG laser) and 20–21 (worked example: minimum pump power of a three-level laser).* ## Key relations A two-level system cannot be inverted (@sec-einstein). Real lasers use auxiliary levels (slides 11–14): * **Three-level laser** (ruby, Cr³⁺:Al₂O₃). Pump photons lift ions from the ground state $E_1$ to a broad band $E_3$. The ions relax in picoseconds, through phonons, to the long-lived level $E_2$ ($\tau_{sp}=3$ ms). The laser transition $E_2\to E_1$ ends on the **ground state**, so more than half of all ions must be pumped before any gain appears. * **Four-level laser** (Nd³⁺:YAG). The laser transition ends on a level $E_1$ that lies about 0.25 eV above the ground state and empties in nanoseconds. $E_1$ is almost empty at room temperature, so every ion that reaches $E_2$ ($\tau_{sp}=230$ µs) already contributes to the inversion. With a pump rate $W_p$ per ground-state ion and fast decay from the pump level, the steady-state inversions are $$ \text{3-level: }\ \frac{N_2-N_1}{N_0}=\frac{W_p\tau_{sp}-1}{W_p\tau_{sp}+1},\qquad \text{4-level: }\ \frac{N_2-N_1}{N_0}=\frac{W_p(\tau_{21}-\tau_{10})}{1+W_p(\tau_{21}+\tau_{10})}\approx W_p\tau_{21}. $$ The three-level system needs $W_p\tau_{sp}>1$: every ion must be pumped faster than it decays, which gives the minimum pump power of slide 20, $$ \frac{P_{p,\min}}{V}=\frac{N_0}{2}\,\frac{h\nu_{13}}{\tau_{sp}}. $$ ## Inversion versus pump rate ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof lv = Inputs.form({ lw: Inputs.range([-3, 2], {value: 0.3, step: 0.02, label: "log₁₀ (W_p τ): pump rate × upper-level lifetime"}), r10: Inputs.range([-6, -1], {value: -4, step: 0.1, label: "4-level: log₁₀ (τ₁₀/τ₂₁), lower-level emptying"}), dth: Inputs.range([0.001, 0.2], {value: 0.02, step: 0.001, label: "threshold inversion ΔN_th/N₀"}) }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false lvOut = { const r = 10 ** lv.r10, three = x => (x - 1)/(x + 1), four = x => x*(1 - r)/(1 + x*(1 + r)), data = []; for (let i = 0; i <= 300; i++) { const x = 10 ** (-3 + 5*i/300); data.push({x, d: three(x), who: "3-level (ruby)"}, {x, d: four(x), who: "4-level (Nd:YAG)"}); } const x = 10 ** lv.lw; const need3 = (1 + lv.dth)/(1 - lv.dth), need4 = lv.dth/((1 - r) - lv.dth*(1 + r)); return {data, x, d3: three(x), d4: four(x), need3, need4}; } Plot.plot({ width: Math.min(width, 1050), height: 320, x: {label: "W_p τ", type: "log"}, y: {label: "inversion (N₂ − N₁)/N₀", domain: [-1, 1], grid: true}, color: {legend: true, range: ["#e34948", "#2a78d6"]}, marks: [Plot.line(lvOut.data, {x: "x", y: "d", stroke: "who", strokeWidth: 2}), Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "#0b0b0b"}), Plot.ruleY([lv.dth], {stroke: "#1baf7a", strokeDasharray: "5,3"}), Plot.ruleX([lvOut.x], {stroke: "#52514e", strokeDasharray: "2,3"}), Plot.dot([{x: lvOut.x, y: lvOut.d3}, {x: lvOut.x, y: lvOut.d4}], {x: "x", y: "y", r: 5, fill: ["#e34948", "#2a78d6"]})] }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false html`
at Wpτ = ${lvOut.x.toFixed(3)}: 3-level inversion = ${lvOut.d3.toFixed(3)}, 4-level inversion = ${lvOut.d4.toFixed(4)}
pump needed for ΔNth/N₀ = ${lv.dth}: 3-level Wpτ = ${lvOut.need3.toFixed(3)}, 4-level Wpτ = ${lvOut.need4.toExponential(2)} → the 3-level laser needs ${(lvOut.need3/lvOut.need4).toFixed(0)}× more pump
` ``` The four-level curve starts at zero and rises linearly: any pump gives gain. The three-level curve starts at $-1$ (full absorption) and crosses zero only at $W_p\tau=1$. For a typical threshold inversion of a few percent, the four-level laser needs **tens of times** less pump. That is why the ruby laser runs only in pulses while Nd:YAG runs continuously (slide 14 notes). ## Worked example (slides 20–21), recomputed > Ruby rod: $N_0=10^{19}$ cm⁻³ Cr³⁺ ions, length 10 cm, diameter 1 cm, $\tau_{sp}=3$ ms, pump band 2.2 eV above $E_1$. Find the > minimum pump power for inversion. ::: {#tbl-ruby .cell tbl-cap='Minimum pump power of the ruby rod of slide 20, and the energy needed within one lifetime.' execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} V = np.pi*0.005**2*0.10 # m^3 N0 = 1e19*lz.CM3 P = lz.pump_power_3level(N0, V, 2.2, 3e-3) pd.DataFrame({"quantity": ["volume (cm³)", "ions to pump, N0V/2", "minimum absorbed pump power", "energy within τ_sp = 3 ms", "slide"], "value": [f"{V*1e6:.3f}", f"{N0*V/2:.3e}", f"{P/1e3:.2f} kW", f"{P*3e-3:.1f} J", "4.6 kW, 13.8 J"]}) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
quantity value
0 volume (cm³) 7.854
1 ions to pump, N0V/2 3.927e+19
2 minimum absorbed pump power 4.61 kW
3 energy within τ_sp = 3 ms 13.8 J
4 slide 4.6 kW, 13.8 J
``` ::: ::: The library agrees with the slide. A flash lamp converts at most a few percent of its electrical energy into absorbed pump light in the Cr³⁺ bands, so a real ruby laser needs **kilojoules** in the flash. Maiman's first laser (slide 12) fired once every few seconds. ## A flash-pumped ruby laser in time The panel above shows steady states. A flash lasts about 1 ms, comparable to $\tau_{sp}$. The figure integrates the three-level rate equation $dN_2/dt=W_p(t)N_1-N_2/\tau_{sp}$ for a Gaussian flash: ::: {#cell-fig-ruby-flash .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp tau = 3e-3 t = np.linspace(0, 6e-3, 2000) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.8)) for Wmax in (300, 800, 2000): W = lambda t: Wmax*np.exp(-4*np.log(2)*((t - 1.5e-3)/1e-3)**2) s = solve_ivp(lambda t, y: [W(t)*(1 - y[0]) - y[0]/tau], (0, t[-1]), [0.0], t_eval=t, max_step=1e-5) ax.plot(t*1e3, s.y[0], label=f"peak W_p = {Wmax} s⁻¹ (W_pτ = {Wmax*tau:.1f})") ax.axhline(0.5, color=lz.PALETTE[7], ls="--", lw=1.2) ax2 = ax.twinx(); ax2.fill_between(t*1e3, np.exp(-4*np.log(2)*((t - 1.5e-3)/1e-3)**2), color=lz.GRID, alpha=0.5, zorder=0) ax2.set_yticks([]); ax2.grid(False); ax.set_zorder(ax2.get_zorder() + 1); ax.patch.set_visible(False) ax.set(xlabel="time (ms)", ylabel="N₂/N₀", ylim=(0, 1)); ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper right"); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Population of the upper ruby level during a 1 ms (FWHM) flash for three peak pump rates (no laser oscillation). The flash is shorter than τ_sp, so the ions cannot accumulate: even W_pτ = 2.4 at the peak, which would invert in steady state, never reaches N₂ > N₀/2 (dashed). Inversion needs a much stronger flash, and it lasts only part of the pulse.](pumping_files/figure-html/fig-ruby-flash-output-1.png){#fig-ruby-flash width=719 height=397} ::: ::: ## Quantum defect: where the pump energy goes Every pumped ion that lases emits a photon smaller than the pump photon. The difference heats the crystal: ::: {#tbl-defect .cell tbl-cap='Quantum efficiency hν_laser/hν_pump of common pumping schemes. The rest of the absorbed pump energy becomes heat in the gain medium.' execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} schemes = [("ruby, green flash band", 550e-9, 694.3e-9), ("ruby, blue flash band", 410e-9, 694.3e-9), ("Nd:YAG, flash lamp (avg.)", 600e-9, 1064e-9), ("Nd:YAG, diode at 808 nm", 808e-9, 1064e-9), ("Nd:YAG, diode at 885 nm (direct)", 885e-9, 1064e-9), ("EDFA, pump at 980 nm", 980e-9, 1550e-9), ("EDFA, pump at 1480 nm", 1480e-9, 1550e-9), ("Yb:YAG, diode at 940 nm", 940e-9, 1030e-9)] pd.DataFrame([{"scheme": s, "λ pump (nm)": round(p*1e9), "λ laser (nm)": round(l*1e9, 1), "quantum efficiency": f"{p/l:.0%}", "heat fraction": f"{1 - p/l:.0%}"} for s, p, l in schemes]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
scheme λ pump (nm) λ laser (nm) quantum efficiency heat fraction
0 ruby, green flash band 550 694.3 79% 21%
1 ruby, blue flash band 410 694.3 59% 41%
2 Nd:YAG, flash lamp (avg.) 600 1064.0 56% 44%
3 Nd:YAG, diode at 808 nm 808 1064.0 76% 24%
4 Nd:YAG, diode at 885 nm (direct) 885 1064.0 83% 17%

``` ::: ::: Diode pumping into a narrow absorption line (808 nm for Nd³⁺) replaced flash lamps in most solid-state lasers. It wastes less pump light and less heat. Pumping directly into the upper laser level (885 nm, 1480 nm) cuts the heat further but makes the system **quasi-three-level**: the pump also stimulates emission back down. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Going further - **Quasi-three-level media** (Yb³⁺, Er³⁺). The lower laser level lies only a few $k_BT$ above the ground state and is thermally populated. Write $N_1$ with a Boltzmann factor and find how the threshold depends on temperature. Why are Yb lasers cooled to reach high power? - **Lasers without pump levels.** Ti:sapphire and dye lasers are "vibronic" four-level systems: the lower level is a vibrational state of the ground electronic level. Their gain spans 650–1100 nm (Ti:sapphire), the basis of femtosecond lasers (@sec-pulsed). - **Thermal lensing.** The heat of the quantum defect creates a radial temperature profile and a positive lens in the rod. Estimate the focal length of a Nd:YAG rod absorbing 50 W ($dn/dT=7\times10^{-6}$ K⁻¹, thermal conductivity 13 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹). ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Complements - T. H. Maiman, "Stimulated optical radiation in ruby", *Nature* 187, 493 (1960): one page that started the field. - Kasap, sec. 4.2–4.3; Koechner, *Solid-State Laser Engineering*, 6th ed., ch. 1–2 and 6 (pumping). ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Repeat the ruby example for a Nd:YAG rod of the same size ($N_0=1.4\times10^{20}$ cm⁻³, pump 808 nm, $\tau=230$ µs) that needs an inversion of $10^{17}$ cm⁻³. Compare the pump powers. 2. In the panel, set $\tau_{10}/\tau_{21}=0.1$. What happens to the four-level inversion at high pump rates? Explain the limit. 3. For the 3-level system, at what $W_p\tau$ is half of the ions above $E_1$ in excess (inversion 0.5)? 4. A Nd:YAG laser emits 10 W at 1064 nm when pumped with 25 W at 808 nm. What fraction of the losses is the quantum defect?
